Among the various spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) seen by Sudhana—such as the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha and the bhikṣu Supratiṣṭhita—who manifest in the bodies of śrāvakas to preach the Separate and Perfect Teachings, they preach the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings when the capacities of those of the Two Vehicles are triggered.
Having already abided in the inconceivable dharma-gate, what is there that cannot be expounded?
This corresponds here to the four propositions regarding the human dharma.
Third, "Next, citing the Mahā... and below, concerns the ability to manifest the dharma.

The preceding section generally summarized the Dharma to clarify the person capable of manifestation; now, this section specifically demonstrates the skillful means of the Small Vehicle, citing the four kinds of wisdom from the Mahāyāna Sūtra that contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination to attain the fruits of the four vehicles.

If one cultivates the distinct contemplation (bie guan), one employs the four wisdoms in succession to contemplate conditions; if one cultivates the perfect contemplation (yuan guan), one employs the wisdom of the four causal conditions with a single mind, while in each instance giving rise to vows to deliver all sentient beings.

Not grasping the four marks and not abandoning the four dharmas—because they are not grasped, they are not existent; because they are not abandoned, they are not empty. This simultaneous negation of the two extremes constitutes the vow of non-conditioning, while the simultaneous illumination of arising and dharmas constitutes the four types of compassion.
Now that the practices and vows have been fulfilled, they manifest throughout the entire dharma-realm in four forms and voices to universally respond to all beings.
Among these four, specifically, the wisdom of ultimate reality (*jñāna*) is taken as the capacity that manifests the dharmas.
IV. Regarding the section "Question" below, there are two parts consisting of a preliminary analysis;
first, the question.

Following the previous analysis that the bodies of the ten realms respond to the capacities of the ten realms—wherein the one and the many interact to form four permutations—it was established that ultimately there is a Buddha who delivers beings within the Buddha-realm; hence, the present question arises.
The response, "Those who have attained the first stage through Equal Enlightenment," refers to the meaning of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).

This is because the principle of the six stages of "being already Buddha" (*liuji fo*) in the Perfect Teaching is too broad, whereas the meaning of the Buddha-realm upon ascending the stages is clearly manifested in the Separate Teaching.

Why is this? Because in the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the three levels of the Sages employ the contemplative methods cultivated within the Three Vehicles; upon entering the stages (bhūmis) and realizing the Middle Way, they transcend the nine realms entirely, for their initial and fundamental aspects, as well as their essence and function, are identical to those of the Buddha.

However, this is but a partial realization; since afflictions must vary in thickness and wisdom in depth, it is for this reason that Buddhas who manifest transformation for others at higher stages deliver those at lower stages who have attained the Buddha of self-cultivation.

To use an analogy: when a master among men guides his disciples, one must know that the Buddha who performs the guiding may manifest in the eight phases of enlightenment or sit upon the Flower King throne; however, the Buddha who is guided must necessarily take on a causal body. Because the Buddha’s majestic demeanor is not something acquired through the characteristics of dharmas, the Buddhas of all four teachings possess no "teacher-dependent wisdom" (śāstrajñāna).

Furthermore, for the time being, it is generally said that Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) transcends the First Ground; however, if the original basis is low while the trace is high, one may say that the First Ground transcends Equal Enlightenment, thereby demonstrating that the Buddha’s trace is the body of Sublime Enlightenment (Miaojue), which results from the empowerment of the ultimate fruit.

Thus, one does not follow the three delusions when being born into these three lands of this dhyāna.

Regarding the ten virtues of an elder, the *Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* (Daben shu), fascicle five, states: "An elder of the world is endowed with ten kinds of virtues: first, noble lineage; second, high status; third, great wealth; fourth, majestic power; fifth, profound wisdom; sixth, advanced age; seventh, pure conduct; eighth, perfected etiquette; ninth, praised by those above; and tenth, venerated by those below."

By lineage, he was a descendant of the Three August Ones and Five Emperors, belonging to a family where the left cap-ribbons were of sable fur and the right were inserted with jade; by rank, he served as a counselor, a regent, a prime minister, a "salt-and-vinegar" advisor, or an "Arheng" minister; by wealth, his estates were as abundant and extravagant as the Copper Hills and Jin Valley; by majesty, his stern gravity was so imposing that order was achieved without the need for strict enforcement; by wisdom, his mind was like an armory, extraordinary and transcendent; by age, he was venerable and majestic, one whom all things bowed to; by conduct, he was as flawless as white jade, acting exactly as he spoke; by propriety, his ritual decorum and scholarly discipline were models for the world to gaze upon; above, he was revered by the Sovereign; below, he was the refuge of the four seas.
Internally, these correspond to the ten kinds of merit of the Tathāgata and the ten virtues of contemplating the mind, as fully elucidated in that commentary.

First, an evaluation of the various jewels.
Second, from "If one relies on... onwards, the explanation of the "price of hundreds of thousands," which has two parts:
first, the question.

The sūtra uses the ornament of worldly objects to represent the ornament of practice; since there are gradations in the adornment of the Dharma-body by the merits of the various stages (*bhūmi*), it employs the relative value of worldly jewels as its representation.
Now, since the rank of Akṣayamati is so high, the necklaces he uses ought to be made of priceless jewels; how could they be worth only one hundred thousand taels of gold?
Second, the answer.
The expression "one hundred thousand" is a general way of citing a large number; it is like saying "the common people"—how could that be restricted to exactly one hundred?
The same applies to "ten thousand subjects.
When defining the *kaṇṭhikā* (necklace) according to its rank, it must be of priceless value.
2. From "If one proceeds by way of" onwards, there is the contemplative understanding (*guan-jie*).

As for the mention of "hundreds of thousands," this uses numerical categories of phenomena to represent the contemplation of principle; how could it be restricted solely to phenomena to determine their quantity?
The neck is that which is adorned; thus, it symbolizes the Middle Way, which is the virtue of intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*).
Since cultivation arises entirely from this nature, all practices that adorn it are free from attachment.
These practices accord with the nature, just as a necklace rests upon the neck.

Regarding the term "understanding," although a bodhisattva possesses all the merits of seeking the supreme above and transforming those below, there is never a time when this is not in accord with constant relinquishment;
because he wishes to demonstrate to sentient beings the practice of constant relinquishment, he unties his jeweled necklace and gives it as a gift.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* primarily elucidates the principle of the "Garland Ornament of Practice. Regarding "one ground accomplishing ten thousand":

this refers to the thorough realization of the single mind—that within the hundred dharmas of the ten realms, the thousand dharmas of the hundred realms, and the ten thousand dharmas of the thousand realms, these ten thousand dharmas are inherently complete by nature. When the entirety of this nature gives rise to cultivation, it is termed the "ten thousand virtues. These include the three trainings, the six perfections, samādhis, dhāraṇīs, supernatural powers, wisdom, the four immeasurables, the four means of integration, the three mindfulnesses, the eight liberations, the ten powers, and the fearlessnesses; all of these can be partially realized throughout the ten grounds.
Ten thousand virtues thus constitute one hundred thousand; therefore, we know that the mention of numbers does not refer exclusively to material things.
Second, regarding "Dharma-giving" (*dharmadāna*) below, this explains Dharma-giving in two parts:
first, the traditional interpretation which emphasizes the gravity of Dharma-giving.

If one practices the gift of material wealth because of a deep reverence for the sublime Dharma, then material wealth and the Dharma would be divided into two separate streams; how could such a principle be correct?
Second, I shall now clarify the gift of material wealth in accordance with the Dharma.

The Dharma is the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), the perfect and eternal essence of the three truths; now, since the substance of wealth is itself this nature, and all phenomena proceed toward wealth as their ultimate destination, there is no going beyond this.
Since even wealth cannot be apprehended, how could there be any "going" or "not going"?
Therefore, wealth and the Dharma are neither two nor distinct;
there is no Dharma outside of wealth, and no wealth outside of the Dharma. How much more so is this true for that which is not merely wealth?

Both the giver and the recipient are empty, provisional, and the Middle—there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm. It is only in this way that one is said to give the gift of the Dharma-realm by means of the mind of the Dharma-realm, directed toward the object of the Dharma-realm.

Below the section "Regarding Wealth," it cites the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*, which describes dividing a single necklace into two portions: one portion is given as alms to the lowliest beggar, and the other portion is offered to the Tathāgata Duṣprasaha.
And he spoke these words:

"If a donor gives with an impartial mind to even the lowliest beggar, regarding them as possessing the same characteristics of a field of merit as the Tathāgata—acting out of great compassion and seeking no reward—this is called the fulfillment of the gift of Dharma."

The commentary on that passage states: "This refers to contemplating the field of merit to which one gives, entering the equal dharma-realm where no dualistic characteristics exist, thereby accomplishing objectless compassion and becoming fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas."
"Not seeking the retribution for practicing through conditions" is precisely what constitutes the fulfillment of the assembly for the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).
Given such explicit scriptural evidence, how can the various masters restrict their explanation of the gift of Dharma solely to the act of preaching?
In the commentary on that sūtra, it is stated that a layperson contemplates the field of compassion (*karuṇākṣetra*) as being equal to the Buddha throughout the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Now, since the bodhisattva Akṣayamati is here addressing the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) and speaks of "Dharma-giving" (*dharmadāna*), how could this not be equal to [the contemplation regarding] all sentient beings?
2. From "Unwilling" (*bùkěn*) downward, there are two parts concerning non-acceptance:
first, the literal explanation;
second, the contemplative interpretation.
Non-acceptance samādhi is ultimate emptiness.

With the single mind and threefold contemplation, there is nothing that is not universally shattered: because it is identical to emptiness, one does not accept existence; because it is identical to the provisional, one does not accept emptiness; because it is identical to the Middle, one does not accept the two extremes; and because it illuminates emptiness and the provisional, one does not accept the Middle Way [as a fixed entity].
In this way, non-acceptance does not reside within a single state of mind; it is only by departing from both sequential progression and mere emptiness that one attains it.
One should carefully examine the meaning of these five types of non-acceptance as they pervade all Mahāyāna teachings.
3. Regarding "Reverently Submits Again" (*chóngbái*) below, it refers to a second offering.

The three meanings explain compassion: the first two concern one's own practice (*zìxíng*), and the last concerns benefiting others (*lìtā*). This is still an explanation based on phenomena (*shìshì*).
Regarding "by means of the peerless," this again refers to seeking the reception of Avalokiteśvara through contemplation based on principle. Why is this?
According to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), non-reception means that there is nothing among all phenomena that is left behind; therefore, ultimate non-reception is itself ultimate reception.
Therefore it is said: "By means of non-reception, one receives all sensations.
Fourth, the Buddha’s exhortation;
fifth, the acceptance of the gift.

The original ground of Avalokiteśvara can only be known by a Buddha; however, as he now manifests in a causal body, he must seek the ultimate fruit. Therefore, although he receives offerings, he dedicates them back to the field of merit.

As for dividing a single necklace into two parts, this symbolizes that a single practice must necessarily possess two causes: in principle, it is the "True Cause" (*dharmatā-hetu*); in phenomena, it is the "Conditioned" and "Developing" causes (*pratyaya* and *paripūri-hetu*). The non-duality of principle and phenomenon is called the "Sublime Cause," which is able to accomplish the inconceivable fruit of the two bodies.
The Dharma neither increases nor decreases, yet it is able to transcend the entanglements; for its nature is itself cultivation, and thus its retribution involves both cessation and realization.
Yet this is not achieved through effort, for cultivation is itself the nature.
If this is so, only then can one say that the causes of phenomena and principle tend toward the fruits of the physical body and the Dharma-body.
Regarding the "Response Body" (nirmāṇakāya): because it leads people toward the fruit, it is combined with the [Transformation] Body to represent these two bodies;
once the Dharma-body and Reward-body are perfected, their functional application arises spontaneously.
Sixth, the conclusion of the virtues.
The verses following the prose were not translated by Master Kumārajīva; various masters all maintain that they exist in the Sanskrit original. Jingxi said:
"This too has not yet fathomed the profound intention of Master Kumārajīva."

The *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks* states that "this verse was translated by Śīlāditya (Jñānagupta). Since this verse had not yet been circulated when Zhiyi appeared, he had no means of interpreting it.

Jingxi also cited the passage "it returns and attaches to the original person" within the *Fuxing ji* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning); thus, we know that providing a detailed explanation of the principle is likewise unobjectionable.

Recently, there was the Dharma Master Shi of Tianzhu Temple, who divided the text into sections corresponding to the prose (*changxing*). The two types of question-and-answer correspond like a tally and its seal; now, following his topical outline, I shall briefly explicate this verse.
The verses consist of twenty-six lines, divided into three parts:
first, one line that pairs and recites two questions;
second, one line praising [the Buddha’s] virtues.
The World-Honored One possesses the [major] marks, which are truly adorned by myriad virtues; therefore, to praise these marks is itself to praise his sublime qualities.
Next, the three phrases beginning with "I now" constitute a double inquiry, divided into two parts:
the first phrase contains the two aforementioned questions.
In the prose version, he first asks about the causes and conditions for obtaining the name, and subsequently asks about the manner of the three karmas in their wandering and transformation.
Since this is now a restatement in verse, how could the latter question be omitted?
Therefore, we know that within the two characters of that question in the verse, the subsequent inquiry is implicitly included.
Second, the two lines beginning with "O Son of the Buddha" separately eulogize the first question; the text is very explicit.
Second, the twenty-two lines beginning with "Endowed with" provide a double eulogy for the two answers, which is divided into two parts:
the first two lines are the words of the scribe recording the compilation, which ought to have been stated directly.

Regarding the present verses: some were composed by those who compiled the sutras as an opportunity arose, while others were translated into verse by Kumārajīva; they are interspersed throughout the text without fixed order.
Second, from "Listen! onwards, the Buddha’s response is formally versified, in two parts:
first, one and a half lines add verses praising the general aspiration and practice.
Listen to these two words; I command you to examine them with the utmost precision.
The practitioner of Avalokiteśvara contemplates the sounds of those beings with the threefold wisdom of a single mind.
Causing immeasurable suffering to be liberated all at once is precisely the fulfillment of the practice of benefiting others.
The true mind, being immovable, manifests forms within the three lands; only then can it be called "skillful response.
Because it appears and proceeds everywhere, it is termed "all directions.
These two phrases collectively praise the two bodies—True and Responsive—that have been realized; the subsequent lines then collectively discuss the practices and vows that bring them to fruition.
First, it clarifies that the initial mind’s four great vows are vast; furthermore, it demonstrates that the practice of these deeds throughout kalpas is immeasurable.
Because the vows are profound, one does not regress for a long duration; because the duration is long, the Buddhas encountered are exceedingly numerous.
To act in accordance with the Buddha’s deeds is what is truly called attending the Buddha and cultivating the practices of all Buddhas.
To make pure vows at each and every Buddha-field refers to the specific vows made in the final moments of mind.
If it were not so, how could true wisdom universally uproot all sufferings, and how could the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) universally deliver all beings?
Second, from "I act for... onwards, there is a separate verse summarizing the two answers, which has two parts:
first, a verse summarizing the first answer regarding how Avalokiteśvara obtained his name; second...
The first line of verse provides a general response.
To state the essentials, it is called a "brief explanation.
Hearing the name constitutes the stimulus of the vocal karma; seeing the body constitutes the stimulus of the bodily karma; and mental recollection constitutes the stimulus of the mental karma.
The previous section clarified the response through the unmanifest (the invisible), while the present passage speaks of "seeing the body"; thus, both types of response are fully present.
Alternatively, one may see the body of wondrous wisdom, which does not detract from the unmanifest response.

In the prose section, the general answer to the capacity of the disciples merely mentions their names, whereas in the specific answer, the capacities of the disciples are endowed with the three karmas. Now, in this verse, the three karmas within the general category are reiterated; yet, while the specific category only mentions mental recollection, various literary expressions appear in alternation—this is the artistry of the verse.
Second, from "Suppose" (*yadi*) onwards, the verse provides specific answers in two parts.
First, twelve lines of verse address the seven difficulties in twelve sections;
the first line addresses the first difficulty, the fire, as explained previously in the commentary.
The various difficulties discussed below may all be understood by analogy with this.
Question:
In the preceding prose section, it was stated that one seeks liberation from the three poisons by constantly recollecting Avalokiteśvara.
The Commentary states: "Constant mindfulness is precisely right mindfulness; realizing that afflictions are themselves the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) means there is neither subject nor object.
Why, then, does the present verse say "mindfulness of that Avalokiteśvara"?
Once subject and object are thus distinguished, how could one forget the distinction between the grasper and the grasped? Answer:
The perfectly wondrous teaching cannot be sought through the ordinary mind.

The phrasing appears contradictory, yet the underlying meaning converges on a single point; for it is precisely within the undifferentiated that difference is spoken of. How could there be any distinction apart from the undifferentiated?
Thus, while the text here says "that," the meaning applies to both directions.
If we speak from the perspective of the Buddha’s teaching, Avalokiteśvara is the other; thus, "self" and "other" are distinguished as teacher and disciple.
If we speak from the perspective of sentient beings calling upon that Avalokiteśvara, "self" and "other" are distinguished through the principle of resonance and response.

Master and disciple, stimulus and response—Miaojiao has elucidated that all these are the dharma-realm, each and every one perfectly interfused. Sentient beings are the Buddhas within their own minds, and the Buddhas are the sentient beings within their own minds.

If a practitioner of this teaching encounters suffering or hardship and calls upon Avalokiteśvara, how could it be said that what they are mindful of is different from that which is being called upon?
This is because they know that all things are the Dharma-realm.
Upon reaching that state, Avalokiteśvara is fully present through mindfulness; once this is known, what "agent" or "object" could there be in that very mindfulness?
Therefore, although the distinction between self and other exists, both agent and object are utterly transcended.
Thus, although the verse speaks of "mindfulness of him," it is entirely consistent with the aforementioned right mindfulness.
Question:
When seeking liberation from suffering and distress, one calls upon Avalokiteśvara with the mind; all such karmic conditions are capable of evoking the response of the Sage.
Now, in explaining this recollection, why do you restrict it solely to the Perfect Teaching (Yuan)?
Could it be that those with karmic retributions and other capacities are entirely unable to evoke a response? Answer:

The power of the King Samādhi rescues each and every being from their hardships; in every case, ten stages are discussed, beginning with liberation from evil retribution and ending with entry into the Light of Quiescence. Among the various capacities of the ten realms, who would not receive benefit?
The commentary explains the preceding answer, wherein this meaning is fully revealed.

The verse expands the seven difficulties into twelve, each of which should clearly illustrate ten instances of response and resonance; however, since the intent of the section lies precisely in the *amṛta* (the "cream of cream"), the prose section indicates that the Buddha’s manifestation of his intent and capacity requires only constant mindfulness, and such constant mindfulness must be free from refutation and establishment.

Now, hearing this verse on the repetition [of the name], one might harbor doubts, thinking: "Previously, you commanded that all objects of thought be severed; now you teach the recollection of Avalokiteśvara—how can these not be contradictory?

Therefore, one must resolve this latent objection by interpreting it according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuan): since subject and object are identical, how could there be any distinction between the recollecting mind and the recollected object?
Students should know that although Avalokiteśvara responds to all things without omission, the present school’s instruction to people focuses solely on the wondrous contemplation (*miao guan*).
Therefore, the preceding commentary explained the faculty of intention (*yi ji*), entirely setting aside other paths and adhering exclusively to the perfect understanding (*yuan jie*);
how could the present verse on "mindfully reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara" be any different from what preceded it?
Since my shallow understanding, I have departed from the Great Master’s intent.
I exhort present-day practitioners: whether in speech or in action, do not depart from the Perfect Contemplation (*yuan guan*).
Constantly keep Avalokiteśvara in mind during every instance of suffering and joy; once you have become a wondrous vessel, how could you fail to receive the Perfect Response?
1. The benefit of the single reality constantly moistens [them] from moment to moment.
2. The line beginning with "Or drifting" (*vā plavante*) is a verse on the second water-difficulty.
3. The line beginning with "Or being" (*vā sthitāḥ*) adds a verse on falling onto the peaks of Mount Sumeru.
4. Regarding the line beginning with "Or being struck by," add the verse concerning falling onto the Vajra Mountains.
5. Regarding the line beginning with "Or encountering," skip over the verse concerning the peril of hostile bandits.
6. The line beginning with "Or encountering" (*vā prāpya*) praises the hardship of weapons and staves.
7. The section beginning with "Or imprisoned" (*vā baddha*) praises the hardship of being held in secret confinement.
8. The section beginning with "Curses" (*abhiśāpa*) adds a verse on the hardship of incantations and curses.

Regarding "it returns to the person themselves": whenever one uses demonic methods of incantations or poisonous drugs with the intent to harm another, that person will only suffer the harm if they harbor evil thoughts; however, if they can maintain right mindfulness, the spell returns to the person who cast it.
As it is told in the *Avadāna-sūtra*: there was a lay follower who initially observed the five precepts, but later, as he grew old, he frequently forgot them.
At that time, a thirsty brahmin in the mountains came to him and begged for a drink.
Being preoccupied with his farming duties, he had no leisure to look at it; he then departed in resentment.
The Brahmin was able to raise corpses and command spirits; he summoned a killing spirit and commanded him, saying:
"He has insulted me; go and kill him."
In the mountains there was an arhat who, knowing [of this], went to a farming household and said to them:

"Tonight, light your lamps early; diligently recite the Three Refuges and the verses on guarding speech and body so as not to transgress; by mindfully contemplating all sentient beings with compassion, you shall attain peace and security."
The host followed these instructions and became proficient in the recitation of the Buddha’s name and the chanting of the precepts.
When night turned to dawn, the ghost sought out his slightest faults, but was unable to cause him any harm.

According to the laws of ghosts and spirits, when one commands a ghost to kill someone, that ghost should then proceed to kill them; however, because he possessed the virtue of being unslayable, the law instead required the killing of the one who had sent the ghost. Consequently, the ghost became enraged and desired to harm the brahmin.
The Arhat shielded him so that the ghost could not see him;
thus the farmer realized the Way and the Brahmin was saved from death.
The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) cites this, saying: "This is precisely the passage in the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* regarding 'returning to one's original person.'"
9. From "Or if one encounters... below, there is a retrospective verse on the danger of *rākṣasas*.
10. From "If there are evil... below, there is an added verse on the danger of wild beasts.
11. From "Vipers and snakes... below, there is an added verse on the danger of snakes and scorpions.
Twelfth: Below "Clouds and Thunder" (Yunlei), add "Thunder and Rain Difficulties.
Together with the previous seven difficulties, these constitute twelve. Each must be fully explained according to the retribution of karma, afflictions, the six realms, and the four teachings.

If one discusses that which is symbolized, it does not exceed six types: Mount Sumeru and the vajra are both of the earth element; thunder and rain belong to water; and beasts, snakes, and incantations are all sentient beings, thus representing the consciousness element.

In the causal stage, the Bodhisattva cultivated the distinct and perfect contemplations regarding these great elements; now, abiding at the sixfold limit of reality (*yathābhūta-paryanta*), they universally rescue all from suffering and distress throughout the Dharma-realm, causing them all to abide in the sixfold fundamental limit.

This is because Avalokiteśvara has realized the nature of evil dharmas and attained mastery over evil; only thus can he spontaneously and universally respond to all perils. To state the essential point:

all phenomena of the environment and its inhabitants are the wondrous body and wondrous mind of Avalokiteśvara. All sentient beings take this sacred form and mind as their own objects of difficulty, yet the three karmic activities through which they seek rescue are themselves Avalokiteśvara. Therefore, when the conditions are met, the response occurs instantaneously.
One should contemplate this meaning in every moment; what concern is there that it would not equal Avalokiteśvara’s benefiting of sentient beings?
Second, the line beginning with "sentient beings" (zhòngshēng) is a general verse summarizing the three poisons and the two types of seeking.

All sentient beings are largely afflicted within the realm by greed, anger, and false views, as well as by the delusions of the three poisons outside the realm; externally, they lack the male and female forms obtained through karmic retribution, and internally, they are deficient in the male and female aspects of meditative concentration and wisdom. Consequently, they invite the calamities of the two kinds of birth and death, and for this reason, they are said to be oppressed by immeasurable suffering.

If one can take the auxiliary means of the Correct [Dharma] as the catalyst, one will immediately evoke the power of the True Body’s wondrous wisdom to rescue the sufferings of the two kinds of worlds.
The commentary on the prose section resolves the three poisons and the two pursuits; its meaning encompasses all things, and when contrasted with the present verse, nothing remains left out.
2. From "Endowed with" (*samanvāgata*) onwards, the verse next answers the manifestation through the Universal Gate (*samantamukha-prakāśana*).
This section has two parts: first, the actual versification of the manifestation;
second, one line that anticipatorily summarizes the general answer.
In the prose section, the specific is presented first and the general follows, thereby summarizing the specific;
here in the verse, the general is presented first and the specific follows, deriving the specific from the general.
Thus, the preceding and succeeding sections mutually clarify one another.

The prose section provides a general answer, stating that [the Buddha] "travels through various lands in manifold forms to deliver sentient beings"; now, the verse instead discusses the reasons for this responsive manifestation, which stem from supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) as well as wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*).
If it were not for the totality of the function of the thousand suchnesses, it could not be called the possession of the power of supernatural penetrations (*abhijñā*).

Although these penetrations are inherently possessed by nature, they further arise through the cultivation of vast, wondrous wisdom and skillful means that illuminate this nature to manifest penetration; thus, one attains the sovereign freedom of universal manifestation.
The ten directions have no exterior, and the three lands are not other; without departing from the one mind, they universally respond to all lands.
Second, from the term "various" onwards, there is a verse that reiterates the specific answers.
In the preceding prose section, the various bodies were listed individually, and each body was shown to consist of the three types of action (trikarma);
now, in this verse, the three types of action are specifically demonstrated, and each type of action is shown to be all-pervasive.
This is the artistry of the *geya* (repeated verse).
The commentary has three parts:
first, one line specifically praises the bodily karma that universally responds;
it collectively clarifies the ten realms, yet only indicates the three miserable paths, using the lower to illustrate the higher.
Furthermore, the various evil destinies collectively refer to the nine realms; from the perspective of the Buddha, all nine realms are termed "evil.
Subsequently, the three miserable paths are specifically singled out because they are the most extreme forms of evil.
The nine realms and the two types of death all possess the four marks [of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing]; these are gradually eliminated so that one returns to eternal quiescence.
Second, from "True Contemplation" (*zhēnguān*) onwards, the verse explains the universal contemplation of the mental karma (*yèyè*), which is divided into two parts.

First, the initial line clarifies that the fundamental contemplation of compassion has five aspects; the character "contemplate" (*guān*) is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*), fully elucidating the three contemplations as well as compassion.
True contemplation is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Pure contemplation is the provisional (*prajñapti*).
Because the provisional is derived from emptiness and is free from the defilements of views and thoughts, it is called "pure."
Furthermore, emptiness is inherently pure; it is called "pure" because it causes others to be pure as well.

Moreover, through the provisional [nature] of the inconceivable, the three contemplations are fully realized and one is detached from the defilements of the three delusions; therefore, it is called "pure."
The vast and great wisdom-observation is the middle [contemplation].
Simultaneously negating and simultaneously illuminating, without partiality or dependence, it is precisely the Great Wisdom of Equality.
Regarding these three contemplations, whether practiced sequentially or non-sequentially, there are none that do not function in conjunction with compassion.
The reason why both compassion and mercy are termed "contemplation" (guan) has two meanings:
first, compassion and mercy are themselves contemplations; for example, the four immeasurable minds are called the four types of dhyāna, and dhyāna is precisely contemplation.
Avalokiteśvara observes sentient beings with unconditional compassion; this is called the Contemplation of Compassion.

Second, the Dharma of compassion must employ the Three Contemplations (Samādhis). This is because the Three Contemplations can accomplish all practices: employing the Three Contemplations to extract suffering is called the Contemplation of Compassion (Karunā), and employing the Three Contemplations to bestow happiness is called the Contemplation of Loving-kindness (Maitrī).
Therefore, the preceding text states: "Immediately upon observing their voices, they all attain liberation. Is this not the compassionate mind being applied within the three contemplations?
Although there are two interpretations, their essence is one.

From the initial stage until reaching the ultimate limit, the Bodhisattva’s three contemplations and great compassion never cease from their thoughts; therefore, they cause sentient beings to always aspire to cultivate these and always look up to these contemplations.

The commentary explains that the two types of response—the implicit and the explicit—contained within the prose section must inherently include the fundamental contemplations of compassion and pity; since the subsequent translation of the verse section contains the corresponding text regarding the fruition, those who trust the words of the wise will find them to be in profound accord with the Buddha’s intent.
2. The line beginning with "Immaculate" (wúgòu) signifies that the light of wisdom shines everywhere.
Contemplating compassion through the three gates constitutes the vow made during the causal stage;
the light of wisdom shining everywhere represents the benefit of sentient beings and the discernment of their capacities upon the fruition stage.

The stainless light of purity illuminates the ultimate reality to examine its beginning and end; if one does not shatter the various darknesses of the three delusions, how could the winds and fires of the two deaths bring universal benefit?
The fire calamity that reaches the first dhyāna in the two worlds is a metaphor for the birth-and-death of the Shared Residence (sahā-loka).
The wind calamity that reaches the third dhyāna is a metaphor for the birth-and-death of True Reward (vipāka-phala).

The reason only two [aspects] are mentioned without explicitly stating "water" can be understood by analogy from the middle section.

Although the teaching resides in the mouth, it must rely upon the body and mind as the basis for bestowing the Dharma.
As for the first phrase: because the Dharma manifests its form with the primary aim of rescuing sentient beings from suffering, the Dharma-body is called the essence of compassion (*karuṇā*).

Once the two wheels have been bestowed, one may then transmit the Dharma.
Second, the two lines beginning with "Pouring sweetness" correctly eulogize the preaching of the Dharma by the wheel of speech.
Regarding "ambrosia" (*amṛta*), the Wise One said:
"This is the deathless divine elixir of the devas.

Within the clouds of loving-kindness, the great rain of the Dharma pours down; those sentient beings who receive it find the flames of the three delusions extinguished. In matters involving the courtroom, one stands as if on the battlefield; the mind is anxious over punishment and the life is fraught with the threat of military slaughter. When ancient grievances meet at this moment, a single-minded invocation can dispel all these manifold hardships.

III. The three lines beginning with "Sublime Sound" (*Ghoṣa*) constitute a double verse praising two types of exhortation, which is divided into two parts:

first, one line that praises the profound and wondrous nature of the object of wisdom to exhort constant mindfulness.
Within the first three phrases there are five characters with the phonetic component "yin," all of which represent the vocal sounds of sentient beings' chanting.

Because they are observed by the wondrous wisdom of the Bodhisattva, they all become wondrous objects; because they are illuminated by the three wisdoms, these sounds become three types of objects. When both emptiness and existence are simultaneously negated, they constitute Wondrous Sound; when both emptiness and existence are simultaneously illuminated, they constitute World-Sound.
"World" (*loka*) refers to the two worlds.
Though not distinct, they are distinguished; this is the realm of wisdom within these two sounds and characters.

"Brahma" (*brahman*) is that which contemplates through the four immeasurables—compassion, kindness, joy, and equanimity—and thus constitutes conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); for this reason, it is called the "Brahma-sound."

To accord with worldly conventions and illuminate the capacities of beings—whether they are ripe for liberation or still immature—without missing the proper timing, is called the Sound of the Ocean Tide.
These two sounds and words are the provisional realm of wisdom.

Ultimate empty wisdom transcends the emotions of the nine realms and illuminates the voices of sentient beings beyond the marks of the two periods of time; therefore, it is named the Sound Superior to the Worldly.
This single sound and character is the realm of the wisdom of emptiness.

Although the words follow a sequence, the contemplation resides in a single mind; there is no sound outside of wisdom, and no wisdom outside of sound. When the object and the wisdom merge into one, all discursive thought is suddenly forgotten.
Therefore, "one must always maintain mindfulness" refers to the correct and diligent application of mindfulness.

Although these types of sounds are produced by the vocal karma of sentient beings, when illuminated and perfected by the Great Sage’s three wisdoms as the three truths, they constitute the three bodies (trikāya). Regarding the phrase "constant mindfulness," as explained in the commentary: "This is precisely right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). 2. The single line beginning with "念念" (moment by moment) clarifies that the response of the Buddha's resonance is unfathomable, thereby exhorting one not to harbor doubts.

This merely clarifies the two aspects [of the left and right].

Mindfulness is the profound and wondrous realm of the wisdom of Avalokiteśvara; although one attains the realization of permanence, one cannot avoid the flow of conditioned change. What is called the "condition of reality" refers to momentary mindfulness.

Thus, one should fix the mind solely on this and be careful not to give rise to doubt; for if the rhinoceros of doubt arises, it will obstruct the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Therefore, the sublime virtues [of the Buddha] are clarified in order to exhort one to cease doubting.

However, there are three kinds of doubt: namely, doubt regarding others, doubt regarding the Dharma, and doubt regarding oneself.

first, the explanation of the two benefits mentioned above.

"The Bodhisattva is likewise.
Each [section] of the sutra corresponds accordingly.
Miaole (Wondrous Joy) cites that commentary to explain the present *Dharaṇī* chapter, concluding: "Only when judged by means of the eight teachings does it correspond to the present sutra."

There are many types of karma, which may be summarized into three:

first, contaminated karma (*sāsrava-karman*), which is moistened by the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana* and *kleśa-saṃyojana*), resulting in birth within the realm of segmented existence (*bhinnabhāga-bhūmi*).

The second, untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*), and the third, neither-tainted-nor-untainted karma (*naivāsrava-nānāsrava-karma*), are both moistened by ignorance and result in birth within a land of transformation (*pariṇāmika-bhūmi*).
This is explained in terms of taking birth through one's own practice.
If one acts for the benefit of others, all such actions are moistened by compassion, leading to rebirth together with others.
For a Bodhisattva of the Tripitaka [Śrāvaka] vehicle, their "compassion based on sentient beings" moistens contaminated karma, resulting in rebirth within the same realm of existence as those beings.

The Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching cultivate the compassion based on dharmas, which moistens the habitual tendencies of outflowing karma, allowing them to take birth through supernatural powers within the Land of Common Residence.
The Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body cultivate unconditioned compassion, which moistens inconceivable karma, enabling them to manifest births across the three lands according to their response.

Now, Avalokiteśvara’s unconditioned compassion at the stage of the mind immediately following supreme enlightenment moistens the karma of sovereign mastery within the Middle Way; therefore, it is said that he is subsumed within the Middle Truth (*madhyasatya*).

He responds to the ten realms and is invoked by those in the ten directions, manifesting his body and preaching the Dharma according to their capacities—whether in pure or impure lands, through provisional or true retribution; thus, it is said that he attains mastery over the two truths (*dvayasatya*), which is precisely the supernatural power manifested through the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*).
Those who hear [this] are able to attain the subtle and wondrous merits of both the true and semblance practices of contemplation; therefore, it is said that they are "not few.
Second, regarding the section beginning with "Incomparable," there are two parts concerning the benefits obtained by hearing this chapter:

The commentary consists of four sections, concluding with the statement: "The four *siddhāntas* clarify the arousal of the bodhicitta.
First, the explanation has four parts;
first, the worldly (*loka*).
The two vehicles possess that which is surpassable; these are dharmas that can be equaled.
The Buddha’s wisdom is unsurpassed; this is a dharma that cannot be equaled.

The distinction between large and small dimensions is what defines a "world" (*lokadhātu*).
Second, from the phrase "Furthermore, in terms of... onwards, it refers to human beings.

This uses the number of people to illustrate the Dharma-gate: in every single *kṣaṇa*, there is no lack of the eighty-four thousand pure and impure dharmas, and each and every one of these dharmas is none other than the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
If one practices by forming mental recollections based on various phenomena, one may equalize eighty thousand [dharmas] within aeons;
yet if one generates the mind through the non-conditioned realization of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), one can, in a single instant, equalize eighty-four thousand ultimate dharmas.
To give rise to the mind of true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is the principle of generating goodness; this is precisely what it means to be human.
Third, from "Furthermore" onwards, there is the counteractive treatment (*pratipakṣa*).
Throughout the eighty-four thousand [dharmas], from beginning to end, there is no change: delusion is itself affliction (*kleśa*), while awakening is itself the other shore (*pāra*).
To speak of the *pāramitās* as reversing those afflictions (*kleśa*) refers to their function as antidotes.
Fourth, "Therefore, the Sūtra... and so forth, concerns the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the difficulty of the preceding mind: initially destroying ignorance is truly a difficult undertaking.

therefore, I prostrate. The initial arousal of the mind is the "abiding in the arousal of the mind" (cittotpāda-vihāra). At this stage, one is able to possess the true and responsive merits of all forty-one stages. This mind is so transcendent and superior that it can no longer be equaled; yet this "inequality" is itself equal to the state of Wondrous Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).
Since it is truly aroused, it is the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
Second, from "This is" onwards, the four preceding explanations are concluded. First, the fruit of the fourfold sameness;
second and third, the principle of the threefold sameness. Since fruit and principle are non-dual, how could there be any gradations?
However, according to various texts, the three types of wisdom and the four *siddhāntas* are mostly distinguished according to their respective stages; therefore, fourfold explanations are required.
Though they are not distinct, they are distinguished by clarifying them according to their stages.

Thus, the five grades of *śrutamayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from hearing) immediately transcend the two vehicles, and the accomplishment of the non-dual contemplation makes the ordinary mind equal to that of a Buddha.
The small fruit has a superior [fruit], while the great fruit is peerless; because of this distinction between small and great, it pertains to the world.

From the first stage of faith up to the seventh stage, one abides in the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); having already eliminated coarse defilements, one gives rise to a realization that accords with reality, illuminating the eighty thousand dharma-gates of inherent nature. Since the principle of goodness is thereby established, it belongs to the stage of "leading on" (*tadanga*).

From the eighth stage of faith through the tenth stage, one should cultivate wisdom; internal and external defilements, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are naturally dispelled without being removed. One is able to use the eighty thousand merits within one's nature to counteract and destroy the eighty thousand afflictions of contrary cultivation. Because the evils of oneself and others are thus destroyed, this belongs to the category of remedial application (*pratipakṣa*).

In the first stage, the Abode of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), the merit of the three types of wisdom is perfected, and the three natures are fully manifested. Although all forty-two stages are mutually inclusive and equal, when comparing their difficulty and ease, the initial entry involves profound effort.
In this stage, one first attains the development of the true mind, which is termed the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*).

Regarding "arousing through names": with respect to the designating names, one suddenly awakens the mind of the three types of bodhicitta vows and practices; when confronted by circumstances that are either adverse or favorable, this mind becomes even more fervent.

Because they possess decisive freedom from doubt and stagnation regarding the wondrous Three Truths, and are able to subdue ignorance so as not to be moved by external objects, they are therefore called "initiating [practice] at the level of names."
Regarding "similar awakening": because one applies effort through contemplation, the three types of bodhi develop further than before.

This resembles the mutual functioning of the six sense organs within their original nature (*prakṛti*), slightly akin to the stage of partial realization (*viśeṣa-bhūta-satya*). It is like comparing brass to gold, or like fire being warm first; therefore, it is called the "similar awakening of the bodhicitta."

When the true mind is activated, one activation activates all: it activates all skillful means, activates all contemplative observation, and activates all true nature. These three aspects of bodhi are perfectly interfused and thoroughly realized; they are neither sequential nor simultaneous, yet they are not of a single moment. One thus partially realizes the three virtues and partially shares in the state of the Buddha of fruition.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "At the very moment of first generating the mind [of enlightenment], one attains perfect awakening.
This entire body of wisdom is not realized through another; it is the subtle, wondrous, and pure Dharma-body, profoundly still yet responding to all things.
From the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samāyogi-bodhi*), this arousal [of the mind] exists in all stages, becoming progressively deeper at each level.

Now, in supporting the first two sets of questions and answers, I have provided a brief commentary following the text; it is inherently difficult to exhaustively clarify the underlying principles.

This verse consists of twenty-six lines divided into two parts:
the first verse poses two questions simultaneously, while the subsequent twenty-five verses provide answers to those two questions.
Within the initial question, one line praises his virtues, and three lines constitute the actual inquiry.

Within a single phrase, the name and essence are combined to praise the World-Honored One’s name; thus, by briefly citing his honorific title, one knows that the preceding nine [epithets] are all essential praises of him as the Most Honored One throughout the three periods of time, while the "complete marks" constitute his physical substance.
The marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are "wondrous" (*miao*) and "complete" (*ju*). "Wondrous" is a term of praise, while "complete" refers to the fulfillment of the thirty-two [major] marks.

Furthermore, when combined with the perils of *rākṣasa* demons and ghosts, these six become twelve perils.

First, regarding the single verse on the "peril of fire," the preceding text provides an interpretation through three categories: literal exegesis (*tiēwén*), scriptural evidence (*shìzhèng*), and contemplative understanding (*guānjiě*).

Within the section on contemplation, there is first an extensive treatment of ten phases, wherein one encounters suffering, invokes the Name, perfects the spiritual capacity (*jī*), and thereby achieves resonance with the Buddha.
Next, by means of the two types of primordially abiding dharma-gates—the distinct and the perfect—and through compassionate vows, the perfect benefit of the aforementioned ten realms is revealed.
Here, I shall provide only a brief commentary as a supplementary explanation; the remainder may be inferred from what precedes, and need not be recounted in full detail.
The lecturer should clearly demonstrate the underlying meaning so that the contemplation of the doctrine remains unobstructed and benefits those who come after.
Regarding the term "great fire pit," while the former simply refers to a "great fire," the addition here of "pit" implies that it is both vast and profound, thereby manifesting the power of the Sage.
Even a small fire can cause great difficulty, let alone a vast pit.

Suppose the fires of the kalpa were to rise from the hells up to the First Dhyāna Heaven; even if such a great pit were filled with glowing flames, a Bodhisattva could either blow them out, suck them up with his mouth, or shield them with his hand, preventing them from burning or even turning them into a cool pond.
Next, regarding the single verse on the peril of water: if one reaches a shallow place above, one can avoid the danger.

However, if dragons and ghosts are added, even a shallow place may be feared; thus, encountering conditions for death is more frequent than in the previous case, and the text further clarifies that the Sage’s response is indeed such.
Next, one verse addresses the difficulty of ascending Mount Sumeru; like the sun abiding in the sky, it reveals that the power of the Sage is inconceivable.
However, this is merely a metaphorical assumption—for who could possibly reach such a height?
Furthermore, even if one were to be pushed down and so forth, if such a thing were to happen, there is nothing the Sages would not do for one.

King Māndhātṛ was able to ascend to Mount Sumeru, yet because of his greed for the imperial throne, he descended back to the human realm; if you can recite his name, there will surely be a way to escape [this danger].

4. One verse on the hardship of falling into a mountain of gold; 5. One verse on the hardship of hostile bandits; 6. One verse on the hardship of kings; 7. One verse on the hardship of shackles and fetters; 8. One verse on the hardship of poisonous drugs. Since great compassion and impartial love are logically suited to eliminate these equally, [they should be removed].
As for those who return to their original selves, when they are harmed and call out their names, the karmic conditions are formed and they must be saved.
If the harmer lacks such conditions and their evil intent is naturally subdued, it is not caused by a sage.
Furthermore, there is a spirit within the poison that must possess a person;
if it does not kill another, it will inevitably harm oneself.
Question:
If one harbors an evil mind that regards others as enemies and thieves, why is it that one is instructed only to give rise to loving-kindness (*maitrī*)? Answer:
When the harm caused by a thief is manifest, merely causing loving-kindness to arise already demonstrates the power of the Sage.
Poisonous plots and conspiracies often backfire to bring about their own destruction.

Yet even bandits may bring about their own ruin; for instance, when an old monk of Donglin was struck down by bandits, the bandits themselves stabbed themselves with their swords so that the blade entered their hearts and exited through their backs, while the rest of the gang fled in all directions.
Furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that poison always rebounds upon the one who administered it.
Some explain this in terms of the two functions of "subduing" (dāna) and "gathering" (saṃgraha); this would be plausible if there were responsive capacities (indriya) for both methods.
However, if the one capable of harming lacks both latent and manifest responsive capacities, then even the method of subduing would be applied in vain.
9. The ninth [peril] is the danger of *rākṣasa* demons, which also includes venomous dragons (*viṣadharanāga*).
As there were previously fish, dragons, and demons, this is stated again because dragons and demons traverse both water and land, whereas previously they were only in the water.
Regarding the aforementioned four types of dragons and so forth:

tenth, one verse on the peril of ferocious beasts; eleventh, one verse on the peril of snakes and scorpions; twelfth, one verse on the peril of rain and hail. To benefit those engaged in contemplative practice, one should skillfully interpret these through the gateways of dharmas such as snakes and tigers, correlating them with evil karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) so that they accord with reason.

If one follows the *Commentary on the Invocation of Avalokiteśvara* (*Qing Guanyin Shu*) to clarify the power and function of "extinguishing and subduing" through three meanings—namely, in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), practice (*pratipatti*), and principle (*tattva*)—and correlates these with the retributive fruits, afflictions (*kleśa*), and the dharma-gates wherein they abide within this context, it should likewise be intelligible.
The response to the karmic conditions of verbal action is concluded.
Second, one verse summarizes the two types of karmic responses regarding body and mind.
When the three poisons are fierce and intense and the mind lacks self-mastery, it is termed "distress."

The four classes of beings gathered together and each spoke of their respective sufferings: the pigeon said that lust is the greatest suffering; the snake said that anger is the greatest suffering, and so forth.
As for the woman’s suffering of having no son, it is as described above.
Alternatively, these may be divided into two phrases, corresponding to the mind and the body, which can be understood through detailed analysis.
If one practices contemplative interpretation, there are ten instances of being afflicted by the three poisons.

Furthermore, with respect to the realms beyond [the triple world], one should explain this as a dharma-gate of following and reversing; one should employ the meaning of the preceding text to clarify the significance of the three poisons.

The physical karma lacks the "seed," meaning there is no cultivation of the causes for male or female, nor even the male or female of the Perfect and Sudden [teachings]; this should be understood by referring back to the preceding text.

If the two karmas of mental recitation and physical prostration form the responsive capacity (*ki*), one severs the roots of the three poisons, fulfills the two adornments, and eternally uproots the sufferings of the world within the ten realms and three lands; therefore, it is said that "the wondrous power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom can rescue the world from suffering."
One should also further clarify the fundamental contemplations of compassion and so forth according to the Separate and Perfect Teachings.
Second, five verses specifically answer the manifestation of the Universal Gate.
Although the text here is concise, in comparison with the preceding specific sections, this still constitutes a general summary.
Furthermore, there are three parts:
first, two verses praise the universal manifestation; second, two verses praise the fundamental contemplation; third, one verse concludes with the holy one’s three karmas.
The first section also has two parts:
the first verse directly praises the universal manifestation, and the second verse specifically enumerates those to be transformed.
Regarding the three kinds of *dharmadhātu*, although the preceding text lists the bodies of the sages up to the Vajra Deities, it omits the realm of hell-beings.
In this context, the inferior is cited to illustrate the superior, thereby establishing their mutual inclusion.
Each individual body is explained according to the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), as previously stated.
Furthermore, while the preceding text took the three lands (*tri-bhūmi*) as the objects of application, here the ten directions should be explained by means of the three lands, and so forth.
Next, the two verses on the fundamental contemplation are further divided into two parts:
the first verse concerns the practice and vows, while the second verse concerns the universal benefit resulting from the completion of the contemplation.
The first part is further divided into three sections:
Two phrases distinguish contemplation, one phrase expresses the compassionate vow, and one phrase exhorts one to take refuge.

Through the preceding true contemplation, one realizes emptiness and achieves the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*); through pure contemplation, one emerges from the provisional (*upāya*) and, remaining untainted amidst existence, achieves the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*). This vast wisdom is precisely the Middle Way contemplation; it is called "vast" because it pervades all phenomena, and "great" because it transcends the two extremes.
The essence of the Middle Way is precisely wisdom-observation; because this is its essence, it is called wisdom-observation.
Question:
Why is wisdom named the essence of the Middle?

Answer: In accordance with the intent of this sutra, it takes the union of quiescence and illumination as the essence of the Dharma-body and responsive resonance as its central theme; thus, such a statement may be made.
The three types of knowledge are actually attained within a single mind; they are neither identical nor distinct.
As for "compassion and contemplation" (*karuṇā-vipaśyanā*) and so forth, these are general designations for vows, as they are initiated by taking the truths as their object of contemplation.
As in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, ten dharmas are collectively termed "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).
The subsequent verse distinguishes their benefits in two parts:
the first two lines clarify the light of wisdom, while the following two lines clarify the light of compassion; it is said that these destroy darkness and illuminate the world, and so forth.
Third, one verse concludes by manifesting the three types of noble action (*ārya-karma*).
The thunder of the precepts corresponds to bodily action; the clouds of compassion correspond to mental action; and the falling rain corresponds to verbal action.
The precepts restrain the seven limbs, with physical action as their primary means.
Because the purity of the precepts can uproot the suffering of the three evil realms, they are termed the "essence of compassion.
The wheel of the body manifests supernatural powers, startling and moving the hearts of all beings, much like the crashing of thunder.
To have affection and mindfulness within the mind, universally covering all beings like a cloud, is called "loving-kindness" (maitrī).
To respond spontaneously without deliberation, meeting [the needs of others] without error, is further termed "sublime mental action" (manas-karman).

The wheel of the mouth expounds the Dharma of the true mark as a rain of ambrosia; the three types of grass and two types of trees equally receive its moisture, and the feverish afflictions of the three delusions are thereby cooled.
The detailed explanations of the three types of non-conditioned objects and the three types of non-protection are as in the preceding text.
Each manifestation of conduct and each teaching of the Dharma must clarify the specific and perfect dharma-gates in which the bodhisattvas abide; only then do they possess practical function.
The first section, the "Universal Gate," is concluded.
Third, the three verses encourage upholding and making offerings, which is further divided into two parts:
first, one verse and one line encourage upholding; second, one verse and three lines encourage making offerings.
The first section also has two parts:
first, the single line reiterates the previous karmic response of speech as the basis for exhortation.
Since the previous karmic response of speech occupies the initial position, this single line subsumes both; therefore, it is specifically reiterated.

Regarding official litigation, military affairs, disasters of water and fire, and matters concerning ghosts or tigers—these are rare occurrences that one encounters only when one’s fortune declines. In contrast, disputes and legal contests are common; they are the root of worldly contention. Matters such as wealth, sensual pleasures, fields, and houses are encountered daily; therefore, encouraging others to uphold [the precepts] is essential.
One encounters swords and staves and imprisonment only when one has committed transgressions; military service and royal levies are matters beyond one's own control.
Furthermore, when contending in strength with blades held forest-like before one’s eyes, the ordeal of death is postponed merely by relying on records and registers.
That bandits seize one's wealth is not like the calamities of armies; this, too, is a vital point for exhortation.
Second, the single line and single phrase provide the formal exhortation, which is further divided into two parts:
first, three phrases that employ provisional and ultimate truths for comparative evaluation; second, two phrases that conclude with the exhortation.

First, the Bodhisattva’s realization of reality and its actual benefits are raised as the standard for comparison; because these surpass the provisional wisdom and compassion of the nine realms and the various vehicles, it is said that he "surpasses the sounds of the world.

It is merely a single phenomenon—the sound and dust of sensory objects—that, when viewed through the Buddha-eye of real wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), is the wondrous sound of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
yet when viewed through the Dharma-eye of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), it is the worldly sound of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
This is the realization of reality.
Cultivating compassion based on the Middle Way is called the Brahma-voice; this compassion can provide opportunities and is thus called the Ocean-tide voice.
It is like not losing the proper measure; this is the true benefit.

Compared to the two types of attention on compassion—namely, that directed toward the beings of the nine realms and that directed toward phenomena—how could this [compassion] possibly be categorized as their equal?
Thus, it is clearly established by comparative analysis that it surpasses them.
The final two phrases serve as a concluding exhortation.
Initially, he exhorts constant mindfulness, stating that there are two types of practice—phenomenal and principle—and so forth.

If these phenomenal and principled practices are perfected, one will naturally perceive the two bodies of the Bodhisattva, the form-body and the dharma-body; therefore, this single phrase again halts doubt and provides encouragement.
Next, one line of three phrases exhorts [the practitioner] to make offerings.
The first phrase praises the purity of the Bodhisattva’s three karmas;
because they arise from right livelihood, they are called "pure and holy," meaning that they are collectively worthy of receiving offerings.
Right livelihood is the noble Dharma; because a person who receives this Dharma is called a "noble one" (ārya), it is said that Avalokiteśvara is a "pure noble one.
Second, specific virtues are cited as a means of exhortation.
The two lines following "In the midst of suffering and affliction" eulogize the virtue of bestowing fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*).
"Suffering and affliction" and "the calamity of death" refer to states of dread;
"acting as a refuge" refers to the power of fearlessness.
Just as an infant relies upon its parents, what else could it fear?
He pointed to the previously manifested provisional and ultimate bodies and called them "parents," who protect the children of the three vehicles from the calamities of the two deaths.
The three lines beginning with "Possessing all" [of the verse] exhort by citing the field of merit.
"Possessing all merits" cites the Bodhisattva’s reward-body (*vipākakāya*) as the field of reverence.
"Beholding sentient beings with eyes of compassion" cites the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) as the field of gratitude.
"The ocean of immeasurable masses of merit" is a general praise of the two fields.

"Mass" (*caya*) refers to that which rises high like a mountain; "ocean" (*samudra*) refers to that which is deep and vast without limit. This also refers to the basis upon which these two fields rely, thereby praising the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Homage! This is an exhortation to offer worship through the three karmas; since the physical demeanor (*kāyakarman*) is manifest in this context, it is specifically mentioned, yet one must necessarily possess all three karmas.
In the preceding text, the "necklace" (*hāra*) was omitted; looking at the present passage, they are mentioned alternately.
Furthermore, regarding this exhortation, all may universally obtain the merit of making offerings.
Who could discern the difference between a necklace of a hundred pieces of gold?
Moreover, that which can adorn is itself noble; how much more so that which is adorned? Could it possibly be considered trivial?
For one who contemplates the mind, diligence in bodily action increases merit; diligence in oral and physical actions constitutes the offering of Prajñā to the Nirmāṇakāya;
and diligence in mental action constitutes the offering that accords with principle to the Dharmakāya, and so forth.
The commentary on the verses is concluded.

The Venerable Ciyun of the Song dynasty composed a separate sub-commentary on the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* (Repetitive Verses), which was included in the canon; however, it had nearly not been transmitted in the monastic academies of the South for two hundred years.
In the Jiamu year of the Zhizyuan era, I entered the capital for the sake of the Buddhist teachings and waited for him at Hongfa Temple in the city of Yan before returning to the east.
Treating it as a rare treasure, yet feeling I could not keep it secret, I have finally carved it into woodblocks to benefit those of great virtue who come to study.
Respectfully inscribed by the bhikṣu Xingcheng, abbot of Mount Xingyuan, in the fifth month of summer in the year of Renyin.
